keyVerseText: And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַשׁ (Mash) is of foreign derivation and denotes a proper name, specifically a person or people descended from Aram. Its core sense, as indicated by Strong's definition, is "drawn out," which may metaphorically suggest lineage or extension through a family line. This literal sense enriches the understanding of the name beyond a mere label, implying a continuation or unfolding of a family or tribal identity.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, in Genesis 10:23, where it is translated simply as "and Mash." The singular occurrence limits the range of translation but emphasizes its role as a proper noun identifying a specific son of Aram and the people descending from him. The consistency of its translation as a name highlights its function as a marker of genealogical and ethnic identity within the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: The mention of Mash as a son of Aram in the genealogical record underscores the biblical theme of God sovereignly establishing nations and peoples according to His divine plan. Recognizing Mash as a distinct lineage reminds believers that God's providence extends over all families and tribes, integrating them into His redemptive history. This name, rooted in the concept of being "drawn out," can also symbolically reflect how God draws out His people from various backgrounds to fulfill His purposes. Thus, Mash is not merely a historical figure but part of the tapestry through which God reveals His faithfulness to the nations.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 10:23 lists Mash among the children of Aram, stating, "And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash." The inclusion of Mash here identifies him as a foundational ancestor of a people group, emphasizing the diversity and expansion of humanity following the flood. The word "Mash" contributes to this verse by highlighting the continuation of God's creation through distinct family lines, each with their own identity and role in the unfolding biblical story.
